one_liner: The First Law of Complexodynamics proposes that complex systems initially increase in complexity before eventually settling into simple, high-entropy states, analogous to the second law of thermodynamics but for structure and information.
paragraphs: The paper addresses the paradox of why complex structures—like life, art, or civilizations—emerge in a universe governed by entropy-driven disorder. Motivated by observations that simple systems evolve through intricate, structured phases before reaching uniform randomness, the author seeks a fundamental law to explain this transient complexity. This challenges the common assumption that complexity always decreases over time and instead posits a non-monotonic trajectory: simple → complex → simple.

The approach draws analogies from thermodynamics and information theory, using computational models like cellular automata (e.g., Conway’s Game of Life) to track structural complexity over time. Complexity is measured via algorithmic information content and pattern richness rather than entropy alone, allowing the author to quantify moments of peak complexity. By simulating systems under simple rules, he demonstrates that maximum structural diversity occurs mid-evolution, not at the start or end.

The main result is that complexity follows a 'Goldilocks' trajectory: it rises from simplicity as patterns emerge, peaks when structure is richest, then declines as entropy dominates. This has practical implications for fields like AI, biology, and cosmology—suggesting that complex systems (like neural networks or ecosystems) are most interesting and informative during their developmental phase, not at equilibrium. It also implies that detecting peak complexity could signal optimal states for intervention or observation in dynamic systems.
key_takeaways: Complexity is not monotonic—it increases, peaks, then decreases over time.
High entropy does not always mean high simplicity; structured complexity can emerge even in simple rule-based systems.
The peak of complexity is a universal feature across many dynamical systems, from cellular automata to biological evolution.
Algorithmic information theory provides a measurable way to track complexity beyond mere disorder or randomness.
This law suggests that the most interesting phases of systems—whether in AI training, ecosystems, or societies—are transient and occur mid-process.
eli5: Imagine building a sandcastle: first you have just a pile of sand (simple), then you shape it into towers and moats (super complex!), and finally the waves wash it all flat again (simple). This law says that in almost everything—like growing a plant or learning to draw—you get the most interesting stuff right in the middle, before it all gets messy and boring.
prerequisites: Basic understanding of entropy and thermodynamics
Familiarity with cellular automata or simple computational systems
applications: Optimizing AI training by identifying peak complexity phases to improve learning efficiency
Understanding evolutionary biology and the emergence of life in early Earth conditions
title: The First Law of Complexodynamics
